It distinguishes itself from prior binary voxelizers by supporting arbitrary framebuffer types and programmability via vertex and fragment shaders, tackling load balancing via a tile-based algorithm instead of assigning individual triangles to single threads with global memory atomics, and optimizing the triangle/box overlap test [S1].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence in Source [S1]. Specifically, Section 2 (Related Work) explicitly states: 'Our system differs from theirs [Schwarz and Seidel] in three main respects: first, we extend the pipeline with support for arbitrary framebuffer types, adding full programmability through vertex and fragment shaders; second, unlike their system... we explicitly tackle potential load balancing issues using a tilebased algorithm... Third, we further optimize their triangle / box overlap test.' This matches the claim's points regarding arbitrary framebuffer types, programmability via shaders, tile-based load balancing (instead of individual triangles with atomics), and optimized triangle/box overlap tests.
supported

VoxelPipe implements two distinct pipelines depending on the output mode: a sort-middle tile-based rasterizer for blending-based (standard) voxelization, and a sort-last feedforward pipeline for A-buffer (bucketing) generation [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that VoxelPipe uses a 'sort-middle tile-based rasterizer' for 'blending-based rasterization' (standard voxelization) and a 'sort-last feedforward pipeline' (specifically described as batching triangles by size and orientation) for 'A-buffer generation' (bucketing). This matches the claim exactly.
